newsitem.title: UK: Forward marketing boosts UK wool sales.
newsitem.headline: Forward marketing boosts UK wool sales.

text.p: An extension of the forward marketing system for UK wool has boosted sales, official figures show.
It also provides further evidence that a recovery in market confidence is on the way, according to some of the major players in the UK wool business.
Australia is moving towards introducing a forward market through a joint venture of two major brokers and statutory body Wool International.
The British experience suggests that the influence of a single dominant seller closely cooperating with wool buyers could be the key to success.

The British Wool Marketing Board (BWMB) has offered a six-month forward contract since 1986 but demand from wool users led to the introduction of a three-month contract in November 1995 and a nine-month contract the following February.
Industry sources say the greater flexibility that they provide is partly responsible for the improvement in 1996 sales of UK wool.
By mid-October 1996, the BWMB had sold around 7.3 million kg more wool than at the same point in the 1995 season, 63 percent on a forward basis compared to 55 percent the previous year.
According to spokesman Liz Ambler, the BWMB is now "on target to eliminate all stocks by the end of the season".

Some international merchants say that the UK is in a unique position to sell forward because the BWMB operates as a monopoly, guaranteeing payment to farmers and leaving the brunt of the risk to be borne by commercial agents.
"In a true market environment, forward wools would not always sell at a premium as in the UK," one said.
But UK merchants report that the BWMB was simply responding to demands of a changing market.

"More and more of our customers are being asked to take on contracts a long way forward - particularly spinners - and they need to be able to cover their positions," said Yorkshire-based agent Martin Curtis.

"We are like any other trader," the BWMB said. "We start the season knowing we are committed to buy almost 50 million kg from producers and a steady flow of sales helps to keep storage and finance costs down." Sources at producer bodies Wools of New Zealand and Australia's Wool International cite the commodity's volatility and a lack of confidence and liquidity in the market as the main impediments to forward marketing in those countries.
The two brokers in the proposed Australian forward-marketing joint venture, Wesfarmers Dalgety and Elders Australia Ltd, control distribution of around 60 percent of the national clip.
Wool International is in charge of selling Australia's stockpile of 2.055 million bales.
Sources in Australia say that the new venture is big enough to be able to generate the liquidity needed to sustain a forward market and offer farmers effective risk-management facilities.
The lack of market confidence and the low profile of wool compared to other fibres remains a stumbling block, they add.
But processors in the the UK say the demand for forward contracts reflects increasing confidence on the part of wool users that they can sustain their sales.
"And through their cooperation, wool buyers and the BWMB are helping to secure the future of the British product," one merchant said.
"We've got a good compromise now but I wouldn't like to see any extension of the forward system," he added.

The UK wool industry has also profited from a recovery in the local housing market. Forward wools are of particular value to the carpet trade and buying by this sector has increased in 1996, the BWMB said.
"(Forward) carpet wools have benefitted in price, partly because we can offer these when they are not available spot - at the start of the season before the wool is clipped," Ambler said.
Other wool users are also reporting improved trade as the UK retail market shows signs of recovery, according to John Lambert of the Confederation for British Wool Textiles.
Commentators acknowledge that selling by description rather than objective measurement gives the BWMB an unusual advantage.
Although the Board is looking at its grading methods - for certain types of wool only - this situation will not radically alter, Ambler said.
